options.label: Keratin
options.feedback: The same material as your hair and fingernails.

options.label: Fine bone
options.feedback: Bone is rigid and living; a feather is neither.

options.label: Stiffened skin
options.feedback: A feather grows from the skin but is not made of it.

options.label: Hardened wax
options.feedback: Wax would soften in the sun and melt off the bird.

items.ok_line: The same stuff as your nails, arranged into a very different shape.
items.ko_line: Think of something you already grow on your own body.
items.exp_text: A feather is built from keratin, the protein that also forms hair, nails, claws and horn. It is dead once grown, which is why a bird feels nothing when you touch one and why a damaged feather cannot heal — it has to be replaced. The same protein makes a reptile's scale, which is one of the reasons feathers are now understood as scales taken a very long way.

items.prompt: How does a duck keep its feathers from soaking through?

options.label: It spreads oil from a gland
options.feedback: Near the tail, worked through the feathers by the beak.

options.label: Its feathers repel water naturally
options.feedback: A washed feather wets through like any other.

options.label: A layer of fat under the skin
options.feedback: Fat keeps a bird warm; it never reaches the feathers.

options.label: It shakes the water off in flight
options.feedback: Shaking helps once wet, but it does not prevent it.

items.ok_line: Preening is maintenance work, not tidying.
items.ko_line: The answer explains why a bird spends so long working over its plumage.
items.exp_title: The gland at the base of the tail
items.exp_text: Most birds carry a preen gland just above the tail. They press it with the beak and draw the oil through every feather, which waterproofs the surface and keeps the keratin supple. Detergent in water strips that oil away, which is why a bird caught in a spill drowns or freezes even after the oil is cleaned off. What looks like idle grooming is the bird servicing its own raincoat.

items.prompt: Why does a blue jay's feather look blue?

options.label: Its structure scatters blue light
options.feedback: Tiny air pockets throw blue back at your eye.

options.label: It contains a blue pigment
options.feedback: No bird makes one. Crush the feather and the blue vanishes.

options.label: It reflects the colour of the sky
options.feedback: The feather stays blue indoors, under any lamp.

options.label: The bird eats blue berries
options.feedback: Diet colours some birds, but never blue ones.

items.ok_line: The blue is in the shape of the feather, not in any dye.
items.ko_line: Crush that feather to powder and the colour disappears. That is the clue.
items.exp_title: A blue with no blue in it
items.exp_text: Almost no bird makes a blue pigment. The blue of a jay, a kingfisher or a peacock comes from layers of microscopic air pockets in the feather that scatter blue light back while letting the rest pass into a dark backing layer. Grind the feather up and the structure is destroyed, leaving dull brown powder. Red and yellow behave differently: those really are pigments, and they survive grinding.

items.prompt: What gives a flamingo its pink colour?

options.label: Pigments in what it eats
options.feedback: Algae and small shrimp carry them into the feathers.

options.label: The mineral salts of the lake
options.feedback: Salt bleaches feathers; it does not tint them.

options.label: Long exposure to strong sun
options.feedback: Sun fades plumage rather than colouring it.

options.label: A pigment it makes itself
options.feedback: A flamingo raised on plain feed turns white.

items.ok_line: A flamingo is pink because of its dinner.
items.ko_line: Change what the bird is fed and the colour changes with it.
items.exp_title: You are what you eat, in feathers
items.exp_text: Flamingos feed on algae and tiny crustaceans loaded with carotenoids, the same family of pigments that colours carrots. The bird cannot make these itself; it absorbs them and lays them down in skin and feathers. A flamingo fed a diet without them fades to white within a moult, which is why zoos add carotenoids to the feed. Parents even pass the pigment to their chicks in a red crop milk.

items.prompt: What holds the flat surface of a flight feather together?

options.label: Tiny hooks that grip each other
options.feedback: Thousands of them, zipping the surface shut.

options.label: A thin film of dried oil
options.feedback: Oil coats the feather; it does not bind it.

options.label: The barbs are fused when grown
options.feedback: They separate easily, then close again.

options.label: Static from the bird's movement
options.feedback: A feather holds together lying still on a table.

items.ok_line: A feather is a zip, and preening is the bird closing it.
items.ko_line: Pull a feather's edges apart and stroke them back. What just happened?
items.exp_title: Thousands of hooks in a row
items.exp_text: Each barb of a feather carries rows of smaller barbules, and those on one side end in microscopic hooks that catch the ridged barbules of the neighbour. The result is a surface that holds air yet parts and reseals without damage. When a bird draws a feather through its beak, it is re-closing hooks that came apart in flight. The design was copied deliberately: the same idea gave us the hook-and-loop fastener.

options.label: Shedding feathers and growing new ones
options.feedback: A worn feather cannot repair itself, so it is replaced.

options.label: Losing feathers to cool down
options.feedback: Birds cool by panting and by raising feathers, not by losing them.

options.label: Changing colour without losing feathers
options.feedback: The colour is fixed in the feather once it has grown.

options.label: Cleaning the plumage before nesting
options.feedback: That is preening, and it happens all year round.

items.ok_line: Feathers wear out, and there is no mending them.
items.ko_line: Remember that a grown feather is dead tissue.
items.exp_text: Feathers wear, fade and break, and being dead they cannot heal. So birds shed and regrow them, usually once or twice a year. Most drop flight feathers in matching pairs, a few at a time, so they never lose the ability to fly. Ducks and geese do the opposite and shed them all at once, spending several flightless weeks hidden on water — which is exactly when they are easiest to catch.

options.label: Trapping air close to the body
options.feedback: Still air is the insulation; the feather only holds it.

options.label: Making the bird lighter in flight
options.feedback: Down sits under the outer feathers and adds weight.

options.label: Shedding rain off the back
options.feedback: Down soaks through at once. The outer feathers do that job.

options.label: Giving the plumage its colour
options.feedback: Down is hidden. Nothing sees it.

items.ok_line: It is the trapped air that warms, not the feather itself.
items.ko_line: Think about what a duvet actually does.
items.exp_text: Down feathers have no hooks, so their barbs stay loose and tangle into a springy mass that holds a thick layer of still air against the skin. Still air conducts heat badly, and that is the whole of the insulation — the feather is only the scaffolding. A chick is covered in down before it grows anything else. Wet it and the structure collapses, which is why a soaked bird chills so fast.

items.prompt: Why are many female birds duller than the males?

options.label: It hides them on the nest
options.feedback: The bird sitting on the eggs must not be seen.

options.label: They grow fewer feathers
options.feedback: The count is much the same in both.

options.label: Bright colours cost too much energy
options.feedback: Males pay that cost and manage.

options.label: They moult less often
options.feedback: Both sexes moult on the same schedule.

items.ok_line: Whoever sits on the eggs cannot afford to be seen.
items.ko_line: Ask which of the two spends weeks sitting still in one place.
items.exp_text: Bright plumage attracts mates and rivals alike, and it attracts predators too. In species where the female does the sitting, she is the one who must vanish against bark or dead leaves, so she is drab and he is not. The rule tracks the duty rather than the sex: in phalaropes the male incubates, and there it is the female who is the brighter bird and the male who is dull.

items.prompt: Roughly how many feathers does a swan carry?

options.label: About 25,000
options.feedback: More than almost any other bird, most of it down.

options.label: About 250
options.feedback: Fewer than a sparrow, which carries around 2,000.

options.label: About 2,500
options.feedback: That is a small songbird's count, not a swan's.

options.label: About 250,000
options.feedback: The bird could not lift ten times its own plumage.

items.ok_line: Most of them are down, packed under the visible coat.
items.ko_line: A small songbird carries around 2,000. A swan carries far more.
items.exp_text: A whooper swan has been counted at roughly 25,000 feathers, about four fifths of them down packed on the head and neck — the parts held above freezing water for hours. A hummingbird gets by on under 1,000, a sparrow on about 2,000. The number tracks cold and water rather than size: birds that sit in winter lakes carry the thickest coats relative to their bodies.

items.prompt: How does a bird use its feathers to keep warm on a freezing morning?

options.label: It fluffs them up
options.feedback: Raising them thickens the layer of trapped air.

options.label: It presses them flat
options.feedback: That is what a bird does to cool off or to fly fast.

options.label: It grows extra ones overnight
options.feedback: A feather takes weeks to grow, not hours.

options.label: It oils them more heavily
options.feedback: Oil waterproofs. It does nothing for warmth.

items.ok_line: A round, puffed-up bird is a cold bird holding more air.
items.ko_line: Picture a robin on a frosty branch. What shape is it?
items.exp_text: Small muscles at the base of every feather let a bird raise or flatten its plumage at will. Raised, the feathers hold a thicker blanket of still air and the bird looks almost spherical; flattened, the air escapes and it cools. You have the same reflex in a much reduced form — the muscles that give you goosebumps once raised a coat of hair, and they still fire on a cold morning out of habit.
